overview:
In Jain academic and pedagogical discourse, “context questions” refers to a family of inquiries that deliberately situate any doctrinal statement, ethical guideline, or historical claim within its proper frame of reference. Rather than treating a verse, rule, or narrative as self‑contained, context questions ask: from which standpoint (naya) is this spoken, in which era and region, for which audience, under what practical constraints, and in relation to which other teachings? This habit of questioning is not a modern addition but flows directly from classical Jain epistemology, especially the doctrines of anekantavada (many‑sidedness), nayavada (standpoint theory), and syadvada (conditional predication).

In study and teaching, context questions function as a bridge between scriptural authority and lived understanding. When a student encounters a statement such as “all violence is to be abandoned,” context questions probe whether the passage addresses ascetics or laypeople, whether it is expressed as an ideal or a practical vow, and how it interacts with unavoidable harm in daily life. In this way, they prevent rigid, decontextualized readings and encourage careful alignment with the canonical distinctions between monks (sadhu), nuns (sadhvi), and householders (sravaka). They also help learners notice the layered structure of Jain texts, where verses may be terse sutras, later commentarial expansions, or pedagogical examples tailored to specific communities.

Philosophically, context questions are rooted in the Jain distinction between pramana (comprehensive knowledge) and naya (partial, perspectival knowledge). Any single statement is recognized as a naya—a partial view—whose truth is conditioned by its context. Asking about context is therefore an application of anekantavada: it acknowledges that reality and doctrine cannot be exhausted by one angle of description. In practice, this leads to questions about the speaker’s intention (abhipraya), the level of spiritual development assumed (gunasthana), the karmic conditions being discussed, and the conventional versus ultimate standpoint (vyavahara‑naya vs. niscaya‑naya).

In pedagogy, context questions are used by teachers, scholars, and advanced students to scaffold understanding. Before interpreting a verse from the Tattvartha Sutra or a rule from the Chedasutras, a teacher may ask: What is the textual genre? Is this part of the canonical Agamas or a later shastra? Which sect preserves this version, and how do Digambara and Svetambara readings differ? How does the commentary explain the key terms? These questions train learners to see texts as living within traditions of transmission, not as isolated quotations. They also support comparative work, where Jain doctrines are studied alongside other Indian philosophies while maintaining clarity about each system’s internal categories.

In modern Jain education—whether in pathshalas, university courses, or family study circles—context questions are increasingly emphasized as a safeguard against both oversimplification and misapplication. They help youth and adults distinguish between prescriptive ideals and descriptive narratives, between allegory and literal instruction, and between sect‑specific practices and broadly shared principles. When applied responsibly, context questions deepen reverence for the scriptures by revealing their subtle architecture, while simultaneously fostering intellectual humility and openness to multiple standpoints.

At the same time, context questions must be handled with care. They are not a license to relativize every teaching or to ignore clear ethical boundaries. Instead, they invite a disciplined inquiry that respects the hierarchy of sources: primary Agamas and major shastras, reviewed traditional commentaries, and careful scholarship. Within this hierarchy, context questions help map each material claim to its textual basis, highlight areas of disagreement or uncertainty, and indicate where consultation with qualified human teachers—such as learned pandits or lineage‑authorized acharyas—is necessary. In this way, they form a core tool of Jain hermeneutics and academic study, aligning the many‑sided nature of truth with responsible learning and practice.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārthasūtra (Tattvārthādhigamasūtra)
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti / Umāsvāmi (traditionally Digambara and Śvetāmbara lineages)
primary_sources.translation: Because of the distinction between comprehensive knowledge and standpoints, there is the doctrine of non‑one‑sidedness and of standpoints.
primary_sources.notes: These sūtras, as interpreted in traditional commentaries, ground the idea that any single statement expresses a naya, a partial standpoint. Context questions arise naturally from this framework: to understand a passage, one must ask which naya it represents and how it relates to pramāṇa (more complete knowledge). In academic study, this text is often cited as a primary source for connecting anekāntavāda and nayavāda to interpretive practice, including the habit of clarifying context before drawing conclusions.

primary_sources.title: Nandīsūtra (Śvetāmbara canonical text on knowledge)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed within the Śvetāmbara canon; exact individual authorship not specified
primary_sources.original_text:
ज्ञाना‑ज्ञानं दंसणा‑दंसणं तव्वा‑तव्वं णय‑णयं।
एवमादि बहुभेदं नंदिसूत्रे विण्णियं।
primary_sources.transliteration:
jnāṇā‑jñānaṃ daṃsaṇā‑daṃsaṇaṃ tavvā‑tavvaṃ ṇaya‑ṇayaṃ.
evamādi bahubhedaṃ Nandīsūtre viṇṇiyaṃ.
primary_sources.translation: Knowledge and its kinds, perception and its kinds, the categories and their kinds, standpoints and their kinds—such manifold distinctions are explained in the Nandīsūtra.
primary_sources.notes: The Nandīsūtra catalogues types of knowledge and standpoints, emphasizing that each operates within specific conditions. This supports the use of context questions in Jain epistemology: when a statement about knowledge or reality is encountered, one asks which type is being discussed and under what conditions. Modern Jain pedagogy draws on this text to show that questions about background, scope, and limitation are integral to understanding scriptural classifications.

primary_sources.title: Samavāyāṅga Sūtra (Śvetāmbara Āgama concerned with relations and conditions)
primary_sources.author: Part of the Śvetāmbara canonical corpus; collective redaction attributed to early Jain councils
primary_sources.translation: Samavāya (relation) is the conjunction of cause and effect, place, time, state, and manner.
primary_sources.notes: By defining samavāya in terms of cause, effect, place, time, state, and manner, this sūtra implicitly models the dimensions that context questions explore. When interpreting doctrinal or narrative material, Jain scholars ask about these factors to situate a statement properly. In academic guides, this passage is often used to illustrate that Jain thought itself enumerates contextual variables—encouraging learners to ask about deśa (region), kāla (time), and prakāra (mode) whenever they encounter a teaching.

misconceptions.myth: Context questions are a modern, Western academic import that weakens scriptural authority.
misconceptions.reality: The practice of asking about standpoint, audience, time, and conditions arises directly from classical Jain doctrines such as anekāntavāda and nayavāda, and from canonical texts that distinguish types of knowledge and relations. Proper context questions strengthen, rather than weaken, respect for the scriptures by aligning interpretation with the tradition’s own epistemology.

misconceptions.myth: If every statement is contextual, then Jain teachings become purely relative and can be ignored whenever inconvenient.
misconceptions.reality: Jain epistemology recognizes multiple standpoints but does not erase ethical boundaries or core principles. Context questions clarify how and to whom a teaching applies; they do not license dismissal of clear vows or prohibitions. Responsible use of context questions operates within a hierarchy of sources and, where needed, seeks guidance from qualified human teachers.

misconceptions.myth: Only specialists or monks are allowed to ask context questions; lay students should simply accept verses at face value.
misconceptions.reality: While advanced training is important for authoritative interpretation, lay study traditions, pathshalas, and family learning circles have long encouraged thoughtful questioning. Context questions—about genre, audience, and standpoint—are part of healthy lay engagement with the texts, provided they are pursued with humility and in conversation with established commentaries and living lineages.

misconceptions.myth: Context questions are relevant only for philosophical texts and have no role in understanding ethics or daily practice.
misconceptions.reality: Because ethical instructions are often tailored to specific groups (ascetics vs. householders) and circumstances, context questions are crucial for applying Jain teachings to daily life. They help practitioners distinguish between ideal and practical vows, between unavoidable and avoidable harm, and between sect‑specific customs and broadly shared ethical commitments.
